name: Iron Cross
label: Dischord
lede: America's first Oi! band came out of the Dischord House, put three songs on Flex Your Head, and wrote one called "Crucified" that outran them by decades and ended up in hands they never wanted.

eras.title: A Baltimore skin in the Dischord House
eras.text: Sab Grey came down to DC shows with the Baltimore punk crowd and, by the time he moved to town in 1981, had traded punk for an Oi! look. He lived at the Dischord House, ran with an early scene he remembers for drinking and fighting, and found two younger players who'd already been in several bands together.

years.p: Sab Grey, a regular at early D.C. shows by way of Baltimore, becomes one of the many residents of the Dischord House in Arlington.

Sab Grey teams with drummer [[Dante Ferrando|98b1e2a2-3868-47f0-b905-35637b5a902f]], guitarist [[Mark Haggerty|235b9917-3f4c-4670-ade3-d94f8e45a044]] and bassist John Falls. Ferrando is the one member with spiked punk hair; the rest are skinheads.
years.xp:
Dischord dates the start to early 1981; Wikipedia says 1980, when Ferrando met Grey. Wikipedia counts them as the first band in the United States to take on both the skinhead look and the sound of Oi!.

Grey has said the early DC scene was far rowdier than its clean-living reputation: drinking, smoking and fighting.

years.p: Original bassist John Falls leaves Iron Cross after an early show at American University. [[Cynthia Connolly|bd50eae3-e00b-48c4-9b7d-4a7a41150ce2]] and [[Chris Haskett|963aeedd-f71e-4b09-8e65-76fc9ddde611]] pass through before [[Wendel Blow|6604fe5c-1a16-4689-861e-8658255eaf09]] joins from the just-ended [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].

eras.title: Flex Your Head, and the first exits
eras.text: Dischord's Flex Your Head put Iron Cross in front of a national audience alongside Minor Threat and SOA. Almost as fast, the band's crowd started to worry its own members, and the original lineup came apart.

years.h: Iron Cross's three songs on Flex Your Head
years.p: "War Games", "New Breed" and "Live for Now" introduce Iron Cross nationally on Dischord No. 7, next to [[Minor Threat|09037f07-42bc-46ac-a1ee-37f834451fee]] and [[SOA|e54cb250-3502-4c32-9482-70488bd9a8cb]].
years.xp: The three songs were recorded at C.A.B. Studios rather than Inner Ear.

years.p: The EP carries Iron Cross's signature song, "Crucified". It's since been reissued through TKO, which Dischord distributes.

years.h: Wendel Blow is first out of Iron Cross
years.p: Per Dischord, bassist Wendel Blow is the first member to leave. Original D.C. skin John Dunn and later Paul Cleary take turns on bass.

years.h: Dante Ferrando and Mark Haggerty quit to form Gray Matter
years.p: Uneasy that Iron Cross's image was reflecting its violent supporters more than its members, Ferrando and Haggerty quit and form [[Gray Matter|c9065214-ba09-4c2c-b341-35713b702264]]. From here it's a revolving lineup around Sab Grey.

years.h: Iron Cross's second EP, Hated and Proud

eras.title: Branded the enemy
eras.text: The name and the shaved heads drew accusations of fascism that the band always denied. By 1985 Grey was the last original member and the fight wasn't worth it anymore.

q: They just decided one day that we were the enemy and that was it.
years.h: Maximum Rocknroll brands Iron Cross fascists
years.p: Critics, led by Tim Yohannan's Maximum Rocknroll, cast Iron Cross as fascists. The band always denied it and said they hated Nazis.
years.xp:
Sab Grey's complaint, repeated in a 2012 Vice interview, is that nobody asked. He told a 1984 zine that the people calling them Nazis were the ones prejudiced against them. Wikipedia notes he felt the intolerance ran toward him for being white.

Both things were true at once: the band denied any fascist politics, and the name and look made them a magnet for people who had them. It's exactly what drove Dante Ferrando and Mark Haggerty out.

years.h: Sab Grey breaks up Iron Cross
years.p: With the fascism accusations still following the band, Sab Grey ends Iron Cross. In 1986 he moves to England and plays rockabilly and country.

eras.title: "Crucified" leaves home
eras.text: The song Iron Cross is remembered for became somebody else's anthem. Agnostic Front made it a New York hardcore staple, and it spread to skinheads of every politics, including the ones Iron Cross said they hated.

years.cap: Agnostic Front's Liberty and Justice For... (1987) carries their studio version of "Crucified"
years.p: The New York band had played Iron Cross's "Crucified" live since the mid-'80s; it lands on Liberty and Justice For... and later Something's Gotta Give.
years.xp:
Wikipedia describes the song as an anthem for communist, anarchist and apolitical skinheads and for white power sympathizers alike. A song about being judged for how you look became, for some, a flag to wave.

[[The Business|9557fdd9-41a0-4029-84d9-cb3ae944ee8a]] covered it too.

eras.title: Grey keeps the name alive
eras.text: Back in the States, Grey started the Royal Americans, wrote novels and kept bringing Iron Cross back with new players. The early records finally came out together on CD.

years.h: Iron Cross's Crucified For Our Sins collection
years.p: A collection of Iron Cross recordings on Lost and Found Records.
A full-length CD on GMM with both EPs and unreleased tracks. Iron Cross is back as a working band by now.

years.h: Iron Cross split a record with Sab Grey's other band
years.p: Two Piece and a Biscuit pairs four Iron Cross songs with three by the Royal Americans, Sab Grey's rockabilly-ska-punk band. That year Grey also publishes a novel, Skinhead Army; Hated and Proud follows in 2009.

years.h: Iron Cross's Est. 1980 EP, and bassist Dimitri Medevev dies
years.p: A new Iron Cross EP on Skinflint. Bassist Dimitri Medevev, part of the 2009 lineup, dies the same year. Wikipedia gives no cause.
Looking back, Sab Grey calls D.C.'s Revolution Summer crap and says most of its bands left him cold.

sources.title: Vice: We Interviewed Sab Grey From Iron Cross (2012)
